auth.apiKeyDesc: A key belongs to one project and travels in the `X-API-Key` header. It is what the SDKs and your servers send events with.
auth.jwtDesc: Login answers with an access token and a refresh token. The access token names the user, their organization and their role, and is what authorizes projects, endpoints, deliveries and everything else the dashboard reads.
auth.refreshDesc: The access token lasts 15 minutes and the refresh token 24 hours, unless the instance was configured otherwise. A refresh returns a new pair and blacklists the refresh token you spent: presenting a spent one again revokes every token that user holds, because a replayed refresh token is what a stolen one looks like. The dashboard refreshes once on a 401 and only surfaces the failure when the refresh token has expired too.
auth.scopesDesc: `READ_ONLY` reads; `READ_WRITE` also writes, which sending an event counts as. A key can carry an expiry date, and a revoked key stops working immediately — there is no grace period.
auth.securityNoteDesc: Only the hash is stored, so a lost key cannot be recovered, only replaced. Keep it in an environment variable on a server you control: a key in client-side code or a repository is a key anyone can send events with.
auth.subtitle: JWT for the dashboard API, API keys for what a project owns.
auth.title: Authentication
auth.usingJwtDesc: Every authenticated request carries the access token in the `Authorization` header:

concepts.attemptDesc: One try at a delivery: one HTTP request and what it resolved to — status, error and latency. The first attempt is not a retry.
concepts.connectionDesc: One endpoint together with the subscriptions that point at it, named as one thing because that is the unit you configure, test and turn off. It is a view, not a record: changing a connection changes the endpoint or its subscriptions.
concepts.deliveryDesc: The obligation to get one event to one endpoint, held until it succeeds or is abandoned. Distinct from the individual tries it takes.
concepts.destinationDesc: A URL you nominated to receive incoming events, together with how to authenticate to it.
concepts.endpointDesc: A URL you registered that is willing to receive events, together with the secret its signatures are computed from.
concepts.eventDesc: Something your system announced happened, with a type and a body. It exists whether or not anything is listening.
concepts.forwardDesc: The obligation to get one incoming event to one destination. The incoming counterpart of a delivery.
concepts.sourceDesc: A third-party provider you have connected, together with what Hookflow needs to prove that a webhook genuinely came from it.
concepts.subscriptionDesc: A standing statement that one endpoint wants events of a given type.

deterministicReplay.diagAlt: Two lanes. In the retry lane, one delivery loops back to itself for its next attempt, keeping its id and sequence number. In the replay lane, an event produces a second delivery with a new id and a new sequence number, while the original delivery is left unchanged.
deterministicReplay.diagCaption: A retry moves a row you already have. A replay writes a row you did not, and gives it a new position in the endpoint’s sequence.
deterministicReplay.diagFoot: the original is never rewritten by a replay
deterministicReplay.dryRunDesc: dryRun=true answers 200 and sends nothing. It returns the target URL, the event type, the payload, the `Idempotency-Key` that would go out, every previous attempt with its status and error, and a plan line: `WILL_SEND` with the attempt number it would use, SKIP when the delivery already succeeded, or `BLOCKED` when the endpoint is disabled.
deterministicReplay.idempotencyKeyHeaderDesc: Every outgoing request carries one so a consumer can recognise something it has already processed. It is <event key>-<endpoint id> when the event was ingested with an idempotency key, and <event id>-<endpoint id> when it was not. The value is stable across attempts and across a retry of the same delivery. A time-range replay creates new deliveries that carry no key of their own, so they fall back to <event id>-<endpoint id>: if the original event had a key, the replayed request's header will not match the original's.
deterministicReplay.idempotencyPoliciesDesc: Per project, in Settings → Schemas & Policies. Whatever the policy, an `Idempotency-Key` that a project has already used returns the original event instead of creating a second one.
deterministicReplay.oneDeliveryDesc: `POST /api/v1/deliveries/{id}/replay` resets that delivery to `PENDING` with its attempt count back to zero and queues it, answering 202. A delivery that already succeeded is refused with 400 rather than sent twice.
deterministicReplay.policyAuto: An event sent without a key gets a random one. That shapes the `Idempotency-Key` header the receiver sees; it does not deduplicate anything, because two identical requests get two different generated keys.
deterministicReplay.policyNone: A key is used when you send one, and nothing is generated when you do not.
deterministicReplay.policyRequired: An event sent without an `Idempotency-Key` header is rejected with 400.
deterministicReplay.replayFromAttemptDesc: fromAttempt=N sets the attempt count to N-1, so the next request is attempt N and any further waits continue from that tier of the ladder instead of the first. N has to be between 1 and the number of attempts already made; anything else is a 400.
deterministicReplay.replayFromAttemptNote: When restarting at the one-minute tier is the wrong thing to do — a target that was down for hours does not need the short tiers again — or when the ladder is nearly spent and you want the remaining attempts, not a fresh set.
deterministicReplay.retryVsReplayDesc: A retry is the next attempt on the same delivery: same id, same sequence number, ladder continued. A replay of a time range creates fresh deliveries from the stored events, with new ids and new sequence numbers, and leaves the originals untouched. The dashboard calls the second one Time Machine.
deterministicReplay.subtitle: Two operations that are easy to confuse: putting one delivery back on the ladder, and building new deliveries from events you already have.
deterministicReplay.timeMachineDesc: `POST /api/v1/projects/{projectId}/replay` takes a window and creates one delivery per stored event and matching subscription. Ordering-enabled endpoints get fresh sequence numbers, so replayed deliveries queue behind live ones rather than colliding with them. POST .../replay/estimate counts first without creating anything, a session reports its progress while it runs and can be cancelled, and a project runs at most two at a time.
deterministicReplay.title: Replay

errors.code2xx: 201 means something was created — an event, a project, a key. 202 means accepted and carried out afterwards: a replay, or a webhook taken in at an ingress URL.
errors.code400: Malformed, or rejected by validation, a schema policy or a fan-out limit. Read message and fieldErrors and fix the request — retrying will not help.
errors.code401: Credentials missing, expired or wrong. Refresh the JWT, or check the `X-API-Key` header.
errors.code403: Authenticated, but the role or the API key scope does not allow it. A `READ_ONLY` key cannot write.
errors.code404: Nothing with that id exists in this organization. Ids are scoped per organization, so a wrong tenant looks the same as a wrong id.
errors.code409: It already exists, or it changed while you were editing it. Re-read it and send again.
errors.code413: The body is over the limit — 256 KB for the API, 512 KB at an ingress URL.
errors.code429: The rate limit is spent. Wait the seconds given in `Retry-After`, then retry.
errors.code5xx: Hookflow failed. The request is safe to retry with backoff — event ingestion is idempotent when you send an `Idempotency-Key`.
errors.errorFormatDesc: Every error answers with the same shape, so one handler covers all of them. fieldErrors appears only on validation failures and maps a field name to what is wrong with it.
errors.headerLimit: How many requests the current window allows.
errors.headerRemaining: How many of them are left.
errors.headerReset: The Unix timestamp at which the window resets and the budget refills.
errors.headerRetryAfter: Sent with a 429: how many seconds to wait before trying again.
errors.httpStatusCodesDesc: What the API answers, and what to do about it.
errors.rateLimitingDesc: Event ingestion is limited per project, and every answer from `POST /api/v1/events` carries the current budget in these headers. The ingress URL is limited per source instead: it answers 429 with `Retry-After`: 1 and carries no budget headers.
errors.sizeLimitsDesc: A request body over 256 KB is refused with 413; at an ingress URL the limit is 512 KB, because what a provider sends is not yours to shrink. One event also has a limit on how many deliveries it may fan out to — past it the event is rejected with 400 rather than delivered to some of the matching endpoints and not others.
errors.subtitle: The error envelope, the status codes, and the limits behind them.
errors.title: Errors & Limits

gettingStarted.verifyLabel: It receives nothing until it is verified

incomingWebhooks.dedupDesc: Providers resend. When the request carries an id Hookflow recognises — `X-Webhook-Id`, Stripe-Webhook-Id, `X-GitHub-Delivery`, `X-Shopify-Webhook-Id`, `X-Twilio-Webhook-Id`, or Slack's event_id — a second arrival of the same id returns the stored event instead of forwarding it again. A provider that sends none of these is not deduplicated.
incomingWebhooks.destinationsDesc: A source forwards every verified webhook to each of its destinations. Each destination carries its own retry ladder, timeout and authentication, so a slow internal service cannot hold up the rest.
incomingWebhooks.forwardDesc: Each incoming event creates one forward per destination. A forward walks its destination's own retry ladder — five attempts by default against outgoing's seven — and lands in the DLQ when the ladder is exhausted. Retries has both ladders.
incomingWebhooks.ingressUrlDesc: The token in the path is the only thing that names the source, so the URL is a credential. Verification is what stops whoever learns it from injecting events.
incomingWebhooks.modeHmac: HMAC over the raw body, read from the header name and signature prefix you configure.
incomingWebhooks.modeNone: Nothing is checked — whatever reaches the URL is stored and forwarded. Only while you are wiring a provider up.
incomingWebhooks.modeProvider: The provider's own scheme, picked from the provider type. GITHUB, GITLAB, STRIPE, SLACK and SHOPIFY have one; the other provider types have to use `HMAC_GENERIC`.
incomingWebhooks.overviewDesc1: A source is one third-party provider. Creating it mints an opaque ingress URL; what arrives there is verified, stored as an incoming event, and forwarded to every destination on the source.
incomingWebhooks.providerTypes: Provider types: `GENERIC`, GITHUB, GITLAB, STRIPE, SHOPIFY, SLACK, TWILIO, CUSTOM.
incomingWebhooks.resp202: Accepted and stored. The body carries the request id.
incomingWebhooks.resp401: Verification is configured and the signature did not check out. Nothing is stored.
incomingWebhooks.resp410: The source exists but is disabled.
incomingWebhooks.resp413: The body is larger than 512 KB.
incomingWebhooks.resp429: The source's per-second limit is spent; `Retry-After` is 1. The limiter fails closed, so it also answers this when Redis is unreachable.

retries.ageCapDesc: A delivery outstanding longer than 96 hours, or a forward longer than 24, is moved to the DLQ whatever its attempt count says. It exists for obligations that stopped moving — never rescheduled, never claimed — rather than for ones that are failing on the ladder, which the ladder itself ends.
retries.diagramAlt: State diagram. `PENDING` is claimed into PROCESSING, which ends in `SUCCESS` on a `2xx`, in `FAILED` on a result not worth retrying, or in DLQ once the retry ladder is exhausted. A retryable failure sends it back to `PENDING`, and a deferral sends it back without spending an attempt. A dashed arrow marks the second way into DLQ: the age cap.
retries.diagramCaption: The transitions a delivery makes on its own. The manual ones — replaying it, retrying it from Failed Messages — are described below.
retries.dlqDesc: The DLQ — Failed Messages on screen — is where a delivery lands once Hookflow has abandoned it: kept for a person to decide about, not deleted. `GET /api/v1/projects/{projectId}/dlq` is the same list the screen shows: the endpoint URL, the event type, how many attempts were made, the last error and when it was given up on.
retries.dlqRetryDesc: Retrying a failed message resets that same delivery — `PENDING`, attempt count back to zero — and walks the whole ladder again from the first tier. It keeps its delivery id, its sequence number and its `Idempotency-Key`, so a consumer that already processed it sees a duplicate it can recognise.
retries.ladderIncomingDesc: 5 attempts, waiting 1m, 5m, 15m and 1h between them: about 1h 20m nominal.
retries.ladderOutgoingDesc: 7 attempts, waiting 1m, 5m, 15m, 1h, 6h and 24h between them: about 31 hours nominal, up to 47 with jitter at the top of its range.
retries.laddersDesc: Each wait is jittered between 50% and 150% of its tier, so a burst of same-tier retries does not stampede. A delivery carries the ladder of its subscription and a forward the ladder of its destination; these are the defaults when neither sets one.
retries.notCountedDesc: Being turned away before the request is made does not consume an attempt or advance the ladder: a tenant or per-target rate limit, a full concurrency slot, an open circuit breaker, or a delivery held back because an earlier sequence number has not landed. The claim is released and the work is rescheduled. Only requests that were actually made count.
retries.replayDesc: A retry is the next attempt on the same delivery. A replay builds new deliveries from events already stored, leaving the originals as they are — see Replay.
retries.retryableDesc: 408, 429 and any `5xx` are retried, as are a connection error, a timeout, and a transformation that failed to apply. Every other `4xx` is terminal on the first attempt: a 400 or a 404 from your endpoint says the request is wrong, and repeating it will not make it right.
retries.statusDlq: The ladder was exhausted, or the delivery outlived the age cap. Shown as Failed Messages.
retries.statusFailed: Given up on without exhausting the ladder, because another attempt cannot help: the endpoint is disabled, deleted or unverified, its URL is refused by the SSRF check, or the endpoint answered a status that is not worth retrying.
retries.statusPending: Created, or waiting for the time its next attempt is due.
retries.statusProcessing: Claimed by a worker for one attempt. A row left here by a worker that died is handed back to `PENDING` by the stuck sweep, so a crash costs time rather than the delivery.
retries.statusSuccess: The endpoint answered `2xx`. Nothing further is sent.
retries.subtitle: When Hookflow tries again, when it stops, and what it does with what it gave up on.
retries.timeoutsDesc: One attempt waits 30 seconds for the response unless the subscription says otherwise, and a value outside 1–60 seconds is clamped into it. A timeout is recorded as a failed attempt and retried like any other failure.
retries.title: Retries and the delivery lifecycle
retries.whyDifferDesc: Deliberately, and not something to reconcile. Outgoing carries your own event to an endpoint you registered, where holding it for a day is a reasonable promise. Incoming relays somebody else's webhook onward, where a shorter, more decisive give-up is the better one.

rulesEngine.diagCaption: Rules are evaluated before the subscription lookup, which is why `DROP` is cheap and total: at that point no delivery has been created, so there is nothing to cancel.

A rule with no conditions matches every event of its type, so give it a narrow event type pattern.

security.diagAlt: Hookflow POSTs to your endpoint. The request carries an `X-Signature` header holding t and v1, computed over the timestamp and the raw body. The receiver recomputes the same HMAC, compares it in constant time, and rejects a timestamp more than 300 seconds old.
security.diagCaption: The signature is over the timestamp and the raw body joined by a dot — not over the body. Hashing the body alone produces a digest that never matches and never says why.
security.diagSigned: signed: <t>.<raw body>, keyed with the endpoint secret
security.diagStep1: recompute HMAC-SHA256 over the same string
security.diagStep2: compare with v1 in constant time
security.diagStep3: reject if t is more than 300 s old
security.endpointVerificationDesc: A new endpoint starts `PENDING` and receives nothing: a delivery to an endpoint that is neither `VERIFIED` nor `SKIPPED` fails terminally without being retried. `POST /api/v1/projects/{projectId}/endpoints/{id}/verify` sends the challenge below and waits 10 seconds for the answer.
security.expectedResponseDesc: Echo the challenge back, either as JSON with a challenge field or as the bare token. Anything else leaves the endpoint `FAILED`, and verification can be run again. An owner can also mark an endpoint `SKIPPED` to deliver to it without the check.
security.headerDeliveryId: This delivery — one event to one endpoint. Unchanged across every attempt of it.
security.headerEventId: The event being delivered. The same event id reaches every endpoint subscribed to it.
security.headerIdempotency: <event key>-<endpoint id> when the event was sent with an idempotency key, and <event id>-<endpoint id> when it was not. Stable across attempts, so a consumer can discard what it has already processed.
security.headerSequence: The endpoint-scoped position of this delivery when ordering is on for the subscription, and 0 when it is off.
security.headerSignature: `t=<unix-ms>,v1=<hex>`. The HMAC-SHA256 of `<t>.<raw body>`, keyed with the endpoint secret. Carries a second `v1` while a rotated secret is inside its grace window.
security.headerTimestamp: The same value as t in the signature: when this body was signed, which is per attempt, not per event.
security.pitfallsDesc: Sign the raw bytes, not a re-serialized object: a reordered or reformatted JSON hashes differently. Compare with a constant-time function. Reject an old `t` — Hookflow allows 300 seconds of skew when it verifies a signature, and five minutes is a reasonable window on your side too. And read every `v1` in the header rather than the first or the last, so a rotation does not look like a forged request.
security.rotationAfter: So the two deploys do not have to be simultaneous: rotate, then roll the new secret out whenever it suits you. Once the window closes the old signature stops being sent. If you verify with a library that reads a single `v1`, deploy inside the window or update it first — the official SDKs already accept either.
security.rotationDesc: `POST /api/v1/projects/{projectId}/endpoints/{id}/rotate-secret` returns a new secret and keeps the old one working. For the endpoint's grace period — 24 hours by default — every delivery is signed with both, and the header carries one `v1` per valid secret:
security.sigVerificationDesc: `X-Signature` is `t=<unix-ms>,v1=<hex>`. `v1` is HMAC-SHA256 over the exact string `<t>.<raw body>`, keyed with the endpoint secret. `t` is milliseconds, not seconds. The header may carry more than one `v1` — see rotating a secret below — so treat the delivery as authentic when any of them matches.
security.subtitle: What Hookflow puts on a request it sends, and how the receiver checks it.
security.title: Webhook Security

workflows.dagDesc: The graph is directed and acyclic: a node cannot feed back into one that already ran. The builder refuses to save an edge that would close a loop.
workflows.execFailureDesc: A failed node ends its branch and the run is marked failed. Other branches finish, and every step keeps the error it recorded. Nodes have their own timeout, and the run as a whole has one too.
workflows.execOrderDesc: Nodes run in topological order, so a node never starts before everything it depends on has finished.
workflows.execParallelDesc: A node with several outgoing edges fans out, and each branch carries its own copy of the payload.
workflows.execTracingDesc: Every step stores its input, its output and how long it took, so a run can be read back node by node in the execution history.
workflows.howItWorksDesc: A workflow is a graph of nodes. A trigger starts it, and each node's output becomes the next node's input.
workflows.nodeCreateEvent: Announces a new event back into Hookflow, which its own subscriptions then pick up.
workflows.nodeFilter: Tests the payload and stops the branch when it does not match. Everything downstream is skipped.
workflows.nodeHttp: Calls an external URL and passes the response on. Private and loopback addresses are refused.
workflows.nodeSlack: Posts a message to a Slack webhook URL.
workflows.nodeTransform: Reshapes the JSON payload before it moves on.
workflows.nodeTrigger: Where the workflow starts. It receives the event that set the run going.
workflows.sec1: HTTP and Slack nodes call out to the network. Their URLs go through the same SSRF checks as an endpoint, so private and link-local addresses are refused.
workflows.sec2: A step stores its input and output verbatim. Anything secret in the payload is readable in the execution history — mask it with a PII rule first.
workflows.sec3: A workflow runs with the permissions of the project it belongs to and can reach nothing outside its organization.

faq.a1: 10,000 events a month, 3 projects, 5 endpoints per project, 5 team members and 7 days of payload retention. Retries, signatures, Failed Messages, replay, analytics and the audit log are all included — no credit card, and nothing expires after a trial.
faq.a2: Hookflow retries on a ladder — 1m, 5m, 15m, 1h, 6h, 24h for outgoing, one rung shorter for incoming. When the rungs run out, the delivery moves to Failed Messages with every attempt and response kept, and waits there for a person to retry it or let it go.
faq.a3: Every delivery carries an HMAC-SHA256 signature over the timestamp and the raw body, with a secret unique to that endpoint. The Node, Python and PHP SDKs ship a verification helper; anything else is a few lines with a standard HMAC library.
faq.a4: Outgoing: your system announces an event and Hookflow delivers it to the endpoints your customers registered — Hookflow is the sender and signs. Incoming: a provider posts to a URL Hookflow owns, the signature is verified, and the payload is forwarded to the destinations you nominated — Hookflow is the receiver. Both share one attempt log and one set of screens.
faq.a5: Yes — it is the same code. The self-hosted build is MIT licensed with every feature on and no limits on events, projects, endpoints, members or retention. Two curls and a docker compose up.
faq.a6: The dashboard shows usage against your plan as you approach it, and you can change plan at any time from Billing. Rate limits are per second, so a burst is smoothed rather than dropped.
faq.a7: Per endpoint, yes. Each delivery carries a sequence number, and a delivery whose predecessor is still retrying waits its turn instead of overtaking it.
faq.a8: Any of them. Stripe, GitHub, GitLab, Slack and Shopify verify with no configuration — each has a verifier written for the exact header it sends. For any other provider that signs its body with a shared secret, name the header and the prefix and Hookflow verifies it the same way. A provider that does not sign at all can still deliver; the payload is stored and forwarded, marked unverified.
